conclusion.justification: The report states that current evidence does not establish a causal relationship between sedatives/sleeping pills and dementia, describing the evidence as weak, inconsistent, and mixed due to confounding and reverse causation (protopathic bias). Because it treats the evidence as insufficient and inconclusive to prove or disprove a causal increase in risk, the label is hedged.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
**Conclusion:** Your answer is broadly right **if “increase risk” means proven to cause Alzheimer’s disease or dementia**: current evidence does **not establish causation**. However, it would be too strong to say there is *no association at all*.

Meta-analyses of observational studies often find that benzodiazepine users have roughly higher subsequent dementia rates, but the evidence is judged weak/inconsistent. The key problem is **protopathic bias (reverse causation)**: anxiety, insomnia, and early cognitive/behavioural changes can be early manifestations of dementia and can prompt prescribing years before diagnosis. Confounding by the underlying conditions, health status, alcohol use, and other medicines is also difficult to eliminate. An umbrella review of five meta-analyses (30 studies) found effect estimates varied and did not provide convincing evidence of a causal relationship. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10608561/

Evidence remains mixed even when studies attempt to address reverse causation. A systematic review/meta-analysis specifically designed around protopathic bias notes these major concerns; one UK case-control analysis found no association with Alzheimer’s or vascular dementia when a 3-year exposure lag was used. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-018-0535-3  
https://academic.oup.com/biomedgerontology/article/77/5/1035/6354922

For **Z-drugs** (for example zolpidem/zopiclone), the dementia evidence is thinner and similarly observational; one cohort reported an association, particularly with z-hypnotics and multiple agents, but this cannot prove drug causation. https://scholar.nycu.edu.tw/en/publications/benzodiazepines-z-hypnotics-and-risk-of-dementia-special-consider

This uncertainty is not reassurance that long-term use is harmless: these drugs can cause acute cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, dependence, and fractures—especially in older adults. NICE advises avoiding long-term benzodiazepines/Z-drugs for insomnia and prioritizing behavioural/cognitive treatment. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/insomnia/management/managing-insomnia/
